VERDICT 1: REJECT
The first solution incorrectly applies the stars and bars method, treating the boxes as distinguishable and overcounting the arrangements. The correct application of the stars and bars method would yield 3 ways, not 3, due to overcounting.

VERDICT 2: REJECT
This solution fails to consider the symmetry of the problem and misses a crucial possibility: having 1 ball in one box and 4 in the other, which is essentially the same as having 4 balls in one box and 1 in the other. This results in an overcount by 1, making the final count 4 instead of the correct 3.

VERDICT 3: REJECT
The third solution, while creative, misapplies the combinatorial approach. It overlooks the principle of distinguishability (balls and boxes are not unique) and incorrectly counts 6 distinct distributions, which include duplicates due to the indistinguishability of both balls and boxes. The correct count, considering these principles, is indeed 3.
